content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a formulation to learn gradient flows in systems governed by ODEs. Particularly, the formulation includes global approximation of gradient flow using DNNs and an optimal flow formulation of the loss optimization. The work provides generalization error bounds and also includes showing the performance of the proposed approach on standard toy problems.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: 
1. The global approximation of vector fields with DNNs is appealing
2. The paper is clearly written, with minor typos.
3. The generalization error bound establishment is useful

Weaknesses:

1. The contributions seem minimal
2. Does not compare how the estimates of error bounds are different from earlier works that provide estimate on DeepONet based approaches as in "On Learning the Dynamical Response of Nonlinear Control Systems with Deep Operator Networks" by Lin, et al.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presents algorithm for learning the dynamics of a time-invariant gradient flow system $\dot{x} = \nabla f(x)$ from time-series data of the state $\{x_{t_1},\ldots,x_{t_n}\}$. The algorithm models the dynamics function $f(x)$ with a neural network $g(x;\theta)$ and aims to learn the parameters $\theta$ by minimizing the difference between the data and the solution of the differential equation if $g$ was used instead of $f$. They present error analysis in terms of the optimality gap and illustrate their algorithm on several examples.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
- the paper is clearly written and easy to follow
- addresses an interesting problem

Weakness:
- calling the error analysis "generalization error bounds" is a bit misleading for me. I expected to see error bounds for the prediction of the learned model starting from a new initial condition (that is not present in the data) and analysis of long-term error. The current result bounds the error between model prediction and actual state during the interval between two consecutive snapshots of the state that are present in the dataset. Also the derivation of constants in the Appendix show the dependence of the constant $C_0$ to $\theta_k$ which is not clarified how to be uniformly bounded.  
- the result on the Lorentz system is strange. One would expect that a small error in learning the model would lead to large error as time increases due to chaotic nature of the dynamics. But numerical results show precise long-term prediction!
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is clearly written an easy to follow. The presented ideas are not necessarily original. The adjoint method to compute the gradient is classical. Minimizing a squared loss between the model prediction and data is very standard.
content.summary_of_the_review: The presented algorithm follows standard idea of  minimizing a squared loss between the model prediction and data. The role of optimal control is not clear. The error analysis are not really informative and are not really generalization bounds.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work studies the discovery of gradient flow using neural networks. In particular, they modeled the system dynamical using a neural network (MLP) as G(y, \theta), then the gradient flow dynamics can be expressed as \dot{y} = - \nabla_{y} G. The neural network parameters are optimized under the loss function defined as the squared loss of the observed solution and approximated solution. To update the parameter \theta, the key is in computing the gradient \nabla_{\theta}  J(\theta). This can be obtained via backpropagation through ODE solvers or using the adjoint method, which the adjoint method is detailed in section 2.5. Experiments are run in 4 toy simulated systems including a linear system with R^2 state, a nonlinear system with R^2 state, a damped pendulum with R^2 state and a LORENZ system with R^3 state.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
I don't see how the proposed approach contributes to the existing literature on this topic. 

The formulation of the unknown system dynamics as a neural network (sometimes people referred to it as a neural ODE, i.e., \dot{x} = f(x)), and computing the gradient either using backpropagation through ODE solvers or the adjoint method in detailed Section 2.5 are all known techniques. For example, one can find it in the background part of this paper “SNODE: SPECTRAL DISCRETIZATION OF NEURAL ODES FOR SYSTEM IDENTIFICATION” (ICLR 2020) Section 2, and they even had a detailed discussion of the pros and cons of these two techniques; and also the adjoint method are used in the original neural ODE paper (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1806.07366.pdf).  Therefore, it seems the entire Section 2 Methods of this paper is a review of existing techniques and contributed nothing new. Although the authors refer to their application to the discovery of gradient flow while existing works refer to as the discovery of nonlinear systems, there are no new methods/principles proposed in this paper.

Also, the simulations are only implemented in small-scale, toy control system examples without any real-world data or even real-world scale-like problems. Thus, both methodology-wise and experiment-wise, I don't think the paper meets the bar for ICLR publication.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper studies the discovery of nonlinear systems given historical time series data of the system. They proposed to model the unknown system dynamics as a neural network G(y, \theta), and the gradient flow can be represented as partial derivatives of the neural network \nabla_y G(y, \theta). The parameters can be optimized by minimizing the difference between the approximated system solution and the actual system solution. The proposed methods are tested in 4 toy control systems examples, including linear/nonlinear R^2 system, pendulum, and LORENZ system.

content.summary_of_the_paper: Authors develop an optimal control based formulation to train neural networks to predict evolution of dynamical systems in a data-driven manner. The context is specifically to learn an unknown function $f(\cdot)$ governing the evolution of a dynamical system. The authors do this with the help of optimal control formulation in the context of Lipschitz continuous ODEs. Further, authors also derive generalization and error bounds of the proposed formulation. Overall, the presented results are similar to previous works demonstrated in the context of well-known ODE systems.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strengths:
  1. Authors address an important problem of data-driven discovery of dynamical systems while also deriving error and generalization bounds for the proposed optimal control formulation. 

  2. All the neural networks employed seem relatively small indicating the effectiveness of the proposed framework (employing ODE solvers , Optimal control based formulation) in addressing non-linear dynamical 
      systems. 

  3. Proposed method demonstrates effective performance in the context of linear, non-linear (chaotic) dynamics at least in the few examples depicted in the paper.

  4. Paper is well written and organized.


## Weaknesses:

1. **[No Baseline Comparison]**: The results presented in the paper are on fairly standard ODE problems which have been explored by previous related papers, however the current paper does not compare with the previous methods (e.g., [1], [2], [3], [5]).  Comparison (and subsequent discussion of results) with these methods will contextualize how the current work complements, improves upon the previous lines of related research. 

2. **[Lack of Novelty]**: The proposed method is not significantly novel. Specifically, DNNs have been trained in the context of optimal control frameworks (see. for example [4] which employs discrete-weight NNs). The other part of the claimed contribution (i.e., recovering system dynamics from data) is in itself not a novel application, further since authors have not compared with related methods (in the context of recovery of system dynamics), it is hard to understand whether the proposed method is at least quantitatively superior to the other methods. Finally, incorporating ODEs to influence NN training dynamics ([1] being one of the initial proponents) in the current paper is also not novel compared to previous works which have also employed adjoints, backward in time ODE solves to achieve similar effects in learning system dynamics. 

3. **[Limited Practical Applicability]**: The true motivation of the method being discussed (i.e., recovery of unknown dynamical system in a data-driven manner using neural networks) is in practical settings where systems might not be as well behaved and may have noisy data, non-homogeneous behavior, require non-uniform sampling of the domain (due to complex behavior in some local regions of the domain). Yet the paper does not address (or even discuss) any of these settings. 

## Questions for Authors
1. Authors assume uniform distribution of training data over the domain, how would the current method be affected in settings that require non-uniform sampling over the domain i.e., fine-grained sampling in certain parts of the domain , coarse-grained sampling in other parts?  

2. How does the proposed system work in stiff differential equation settings? 

3. Why has comparison with related models like the NeuralODE not been carried out?  

4. How does the proposed model compare with / improve upon the ideas proposed in NeuralODE (including specifically, the idea in NeuralODE of employing ODE solvers backwards in time, using the adjoint method)? 

5. How were neural network architectures selected (i.e., number of neurons, layers)? 

## References:

1. Chen RT, Rubanova Y, Bettencourt J, Duvenaud DK. Neural ordinary differential equations. Advances in neural information processing systems. 2018;31

2. Li Z, Kovachki N, Azizzadenesheli K, Liu B, Bhattacharya K, Stuart A, Anandkumar A. Fourier neural operator for parametric partial differential equations. arXiv preprint arXiv:2010.08895. 2020 Oct 18.

3. Lu L, Jin P, Karniadakis GE. Deeponet: Learning nonlinear operators for identifying differential equations based on the universal approximation theorem of operators. arXiv preprint arXiv:1910.03193. 2019 Oct 8.

4. Li Q, Hao S. An optimal control approach to deep learning and applications to discrete-weight neural networks. InInternational Conference on Machine Learning 2018 Jul 3 (pp. 2985-2994). PMLR.

5. Raissi M, Perdikaris P, Karniadakis GE. Multistep neural networks for data-driven discovery of nonlinear dynamical systems. arXiv preprint arXiv:1801.01236. 2018 Jan 4.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**[Clarity]:** The paper is well written and easy to follow. The employed optimal control framework is a well established (and extensively studied) one, also in the context of neural networks.

**[Novelty]**: The proposed method possess marginal novelty at best as all the main ideas in the paper (a. Optimal Control for training neural networks, b. employing ODEs, adjoint, backward in time solves in conjunction with NNs to learn unknown system dynamics, c. Testing on canonical ODE problems) have all been extensively explored (individually) by other works [1], [2], [3], [4]. Authors have not compared with any of these works.

**[Reproducibility]**: Could not reproduce paper as supplementary material (source code) was not included. However reported results seem intuitive and convincing and no major questions for potential lack of reproducibility exist.
content.summary_of_the_review: Although the authors tackle the important problem of discovering dynamical systems from data, the proposed method of employing optimal control based neural networks lacks any significant novelty. Further, authors do not compare quantitative (or qualitative) performance of the proposed method with previous methods (which have been cited in their paper and are similar) that have been employed to solve the same canonical problems as the authors address in the current paper.

content.title: Optimal control neural networks for data-driven discovery of gradient flows.
content.TL;DR: This paper proposes an optimal control neural network to discover nonlinear dynamical systems from time series data sampled from solution trajectories.
content.abstract: This work aims to discover nonlinear dynamical systems from only a set of time series data on solution trajectories. To tackle this problem, we propose Optimal Control Networks (OCN) to learn the unknown vector field accurately and efficiently. The OCN consists of a neural network representation of the system, coupled with an optimal control formulation. Specifically, we formulate the parameter learning problem as a data-driven optimal control problem. This allows for the use of powerful optimal control tools. We derive generalization error bounds for both the solution and the vector field, and the bounds are shown to depend on both the training error and the time gaps between neighboring data. We also provide several numerical examples to demonstrate the viability of OCN, as well as its good generalization ability.
